notes.bp: A recognizer trained on clean speech should still map noisy speech to words.
notes.wh: Noise changes acoustic statistics and can be mistaken for speech units.
notes.naive: Add noise only during fine-tuning and hope the representation stays stable.
notes.ap: Add variance, invariance, and covariance constraints during HuBERT pretraining.
notes.mech: HuBERT-VIC applies VICReg terms to noisy representations and compares masked prediction with regularizer ablations on MUSAN-noised LibriSpeech.
notes.math: The reported target is WER; relative gains are 23.3% on test-clean and 13.2% on test-other against the noisy-pretrained baseline.
notes.dots: Noise robustness is changed at the representation level before recognition, not only by filtering the final waveform.
notes.ww: All three regularizers give the best reported WER and show complementary ablation effects.
notes.limits: MUSAN, SNR choices, HuBERT, and LibriSpeech bound the result; real conversational noise is not established.

notes.bp: Accent normalization should change pronunciation while keeping the same speaker recognizable.
notes.wh: Changing accent can also change timbre, duration, intelligibility, or words, and parallel data are scarce.
notes.naive: Convert frames one by one using paired data and accept timing and identity drift.
notes.ap: Use self-supervised discrete tokens, nonparallel conversion, flow matching, and explicit duration preservation.
notes.mech: The system extracts source tokens, predicts target-accent tokens, synthesizes waveform output, and evaluates several English accents.
notes.math: NAT, ACT, SIM, WER, SECS, F0 correlation, and feature distance separately measure naturalness, accent, content, identity, and prosody.
notes.dots: The desired change is pronunciation rather than erasure of the speaker, making accent a boundary between language and identity.
notes.ww: The system beats a frame-to-frame baseline on naturalness, accentedness, and timbre preservation, but post-conversion WER remains high.
notes.limits: Accent definitions, targets, subjective judgments, and nonparallel training bound the claim; native-like is not universally better.

notes.bp: Speech enhancement should run on a device that cannot afford a large neural network.
notes.wh: Small models lose detail while large models exceed latency and memory limits.
notes.naive: Compress one large network until it runs fast, even if its structure becomes opaque.
notes.ap: Replace one expensive DNN with simpler hierarchical predictors backed by structured speech-parameter codebooks.
notes.mech: Hierarchically clustered log-power-spectrum vectors drive codebook stages and enhancement predictors evaluated on VoiceBank-DEMAND.
notes.math: The paper compares SSNR and computational cost; codebook classifiers use cross-entropy and the table reports parameter/runtime burden.
notes.dots: This is compression by exploiting speech structure, linking deployment constraints to representation choice.
notes.ww: The framework reduces computation while retaining comparable or improved enhancement scores over the reference systems.
notes.limits: One corpus and parameterized spectral targets bound the evidence; downstream ASR and perceptual benefit are not fully established.

notes.bp: Meeting transcription needs to know who spoke when despite overlap and movement.
notes.wh: Position is not permanent identity when people move, while a single microphone loses direction information.
notes.naive: Use speaker embeddings alone or permanently map one direction to one speaker.
notes.ap: Segment with time-difference-of-arrival cues, cluster speaker embeddings, and combine spatial and spectral evidence.
notes.mech: TDOA detects regions, embeddings assign speakers, cACGMM optionally refines them, and compact/distributed microphone setups are tested.
notes.math: DER measures segmentation/assignment and cpWER measures transcript performance after diarization.
notes.dots: Room geometry is evidence, but position is not treated as identity; this is a core room-channel boundary.
notes.ww: The combined pipeline outperforms single-channel pyannote in reported compact and distributed meeting scenarios.
notes.limits: Layouts, datasets, overlap, and spatial cues bound the result; evaluations are author-reported.

notes.bp: Speech may contain signs of cognitive decline, but health signals must be separated from topic and class imbalance.
notes.wh: Clinical labels are scarce, the dementia class is small, and acoustic and linguistic evidence can disagree.
notes.naive: Choose one embedding or optimize overall accuracy.
notes.ap: Combine acoustic, linguistic, knowledge-based, and neural representations, selecting complementary class-aware systems.
notes.mech: PROCESS Challenge systems combine acoustic features, text features, LLM descriptors, Longformer, ECAPA-TDNN, and TRILLsson embeddings across three tasks.
notes.math: The study emphasizes UAF1 and class-specific F1 rather than accuracy alone.
notes.dots: A clinical marker is meaningful only when the evaluation protects the rare class and controls confounds.
notes.ww: Selected ensembles provide the strongest reported balance across train/development data and individual classes.
notes.limits: Challenge data, demographic overlap, and missing metadata limit the claim; this is not clinical validation.

notes.bp: Emotion transfer should change delivery without replacing the target speaker's identity.
notes.wh: Emotion and timbre are entangled, so an emotion embedding can leak the reference speaker.
notes.naive: Copy speaker and emotion embeddings into TTS without testing information leakage.
notes.ap: Distill speaker-independent emotion representations with cluster sampling, perturbation, and separate style/identity conditioning.
notes.mech: DiEmo-TTS clusters emotion attributes, matches speaker/emotion examples, distills representations, and uses a dual-conditioning transformer.
notes.math: Naturalness, speaker similarity, emotion similarity, WER/CER, and embedding scores measure different goals; ablations remove distillation components.
notes.dots: The mechanism is disentanglement: retain vocal identity while moving the emotional control variable.
notes.ww: The reported system improves emotion and speaker-related measures in the chosen experiments.
notes.limits: Pretrained encoders, datasets, subjective measures, and cross-speaker coverage bound the conclusion.

notes.bp: Detecting fake speech says it is synthetic; tracing its source can explain which generator family produced it.
notes.wh: Codec generators share stages, so a detector can learn dataset artifacts instead of source evidence.
notes.naive: Train a binary fake detector and treat attribution as the same task with more labels.
notes.ap: Organize neural codecs into a taxonomy and use codec-related auxiliary objectives for source tracing.
notes.mech: Multi-task systems on CodecFake+ use codec quantization, auxiliary codec tasks, and balanced source-tracing experiments.
notes.math: F1 is reported for vector-quantization, auxiliary, and decoder/source tasks; the best cited DEC F1 is 46.45%.
notes.dots: The security move is toward contestable provenance, not merely a fake/real label.
notes.ww: CodecFake+ gives initial evidence that codec taxonomy helps source tracing and that balance affects generalization.
notes.limits: The dataset and generator coverage bound the result; 46.45% F1 is not reliable attribution.

notes.bp: A speech model that chooses a voice can reveal social associations even when text does not request gender.
notes.wh: Speech generation makes an implicit association audible through selected speaker identity.
notes.naive: Evaluate TTS only for naturalness and intelligibility.
notes.ap: Probe default speaker assignment with controlled profession and gender-colored-word prompts.
notes.mech: Bark is prompted with two constructed datasets and assignments are counted for gender alignment and inclinations.
notes.math: The controlled assignment counts are an association probe, not population prevalence or a human perception study.
notes.dots: A generated voice is a social action, so voice identity belongs in accountability analysis.
notes.ww: Bark shows gender awareness and some inclinations but no strong systematic bias under the tested prompts.
notes.limits: Two datasets, one model, prompt wording, and supported voices bound the conclusion; this is not a fairness guarantee.
